newsitem.title: CHINA: China talks satisfy Albright, but no breakthroughs.
newsitem.headline: China talks satisfy Albright, but no breakthroughs.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, after her first talks with Chinese leaders, on Monday reported no concrete progress on human rights or breakthroughs on other issues.

But she pronounced herself satisfied with the warm reception she received and touched by the fact that Chinese leaders did not cancel the trip after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, as she expected.

"I was received with the greatest kindness and interest. I am very well satisfied with the atmosphere as well as the substance of the talks," she said after four hours of separate meetings with President Jiang Zemin, Premier Li Peng and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

Beijing was the last stop on Albright's whirlwind nine-nation tour of Europe and Asia and she and her entourage clearly showed the effects of long days and nights on the road. She leaves on Tuesday for Washington.

But Albright, who called China a key to stability in the next century, said she was convinced visiting Beijing on her first overseas trip since taking office underscored China's importance and the U.S. role as a global power.

Her meetings "reaffirmed America's commitment to our strategic dialogue in Beijing," she told a late night news conference. "That dialogue may not remove all differences in our relationship. But it is expanding areas of cooperation and that serves the interest of both countries and the world."

She said expert level talks on missile, nuclear and chemical issues that are a continuing bilateral irritant would take place next month. Vice President Al Gore would visit Beijing next month as well but dates remain to be set, she said.
The two countries expect to hold summits in each other's capitals by the end of 1998.
Starting talks earlier in the day, Qian set a more harmonious tone than when the last U.S. secretary of state, Warren Christopher, was in Beijing last November.

Qian said: "Sino-U.S. relations have constantly moved forward despite the twists and turns (over the last 25 years) ... We are ready to work with the U.S. side to seize the current favourable opportunities, increase the dialogue, extend cooperation and enhance common understandings ... so as to promote the healthy, steady and sustained devlopment of Sino-U.S. relations."
U.S. officials said Jiang, in a half-hour meeting with Albright, was "sober, statesmanlike (and) very positive about U.S.-China relations."
The Chinese "clearly projected continuity" after Deng's death and "Jiang is the core of the leadership," one senior official said.
Jiang, Deng's handpicked successor, said he was "willing to make concerted efforts" with his U.S. counterpart to improve bilateral relations, China's official Xinhua news agency said.
Albright's human rights discussion with Li "was a bit sharp" but he was not "sarcastic, acerbic or dismissive" as he often is, the U.S. official said.
At the news conference, Albright said she made good her promise to "tell it like it is" on U.S. criticism of China's human rights record "and they made clear their position."

"It is an issue on which we have a difference," she said. U.S. officials said she spoke generally about dissidents, Tibet, freedom of expression and religion. She did not raise specific dissident cases but Beijing for some time has had a list of cases about which Washington is concerned, they said.
She said that in the absence of human rights progress Washington would proceed with a resolution faulting Bejing's record at the March-April U.N. Human Rights Commission meeting in Geneva.

The New York Times, in a front-page story on Monday, raised expectations that a rights deal was near. But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "We don't believe that based on these meetings, there is any imminent breakthrough in China's human rights views."

For months, the two countries have discussed a framework under which Beijing would sign two key international human rights covenants, release some political prisoners and restart talks with the International Committee of the Red Cross for a programme of prison visits to China's prisoners of conscience.
In return, Beijing could expect an end to the annual confrontation at the U.N. Commission on Human Rights.
However, U.S. officials have said they do not expect any quick changes in China's human rights policies.
